Multifactorial guard: every source stresses combined chemical-mechanical etiology and independent habit factors (whitening toothpaste, post-meal brushing) produce DH without NCCLs; NCCL repair or lesion presence alone does not establish DH attribution.
governanceNotes: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY with NOT_ESTABLISHED consensus and hypothesizedOnly mechanism despite near-mechanistic biology (cervical hard-tissue loss exposing dentinal tubules is the hydrodynamic substrate): DH expression requires open tubules and varies with sclerosis, bruxism, and individual factors; not all NCCL patients have DH and not all DH has NCCLs, so the epidemiologic support remains cross-sectional co-occurrence.

Treatment-response evidence (tubule occlusion and nerve desensitization outperforming placebo in the Moraschini meta-analysis) supports the tubular mechanism but was not added as a fourth reference due to the schema's three-reference cap; it is recorded here for the human verifier.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: The cross-sectional cohort (n=157) found NCCL associated with dentin hypersensitivity at both single-tooth and multi-tooth thresholds, with DH prevalence 84.7% and NCCL prevalence 49.7% in young adults (Zimmer 2025); the periodontal classification review records root-surface exposure as frequently associated with DH and NCCLs (Cortellini 2018); the SEM study names NCCLs a predominant factor leading to dentin exposure and hypersensitivity while stressing multifactorial etiology (Sakkaria 2023).
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established at the mapping level: the hard-tissue-loss-to-exposed-tubule pathway is the standard hydrodynamic substrate, but DH expression varies with tubule patency, dentin sclerosis, and individual behaviors; the same cohort shows independent DH drivers (whitening toothpaste, immediate post-meal brushing, anxiety) that produce symptoms without the lesion identity; and no longitudinal cohort measures incident DH after NCCL onset.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: A hypothesized hydrodynamic-dentin pathway: abrasive, erosive, and flexural (abfraction) processes thin or remove enamel and cementum at the cervical root area; the exposed dentinal tubules patent to the pulp provide the fluid-filled channels of the hydrodynamic mechanism; thermal, tactile, or osmotic stimuli shift tubular fluid, exciting intradental nerve fibers and producing the sharp, brief pain of dentin hypersensitivity. Symptom expression additionally depends on tubule sclerosis and individual stimulus exposure.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: Cross-sectional co-occurrence only; independent DH drivers operate without the lesion identity; tubule patency and sclerosis vary between patients with identical lesions; and no incident-cohort or treatment-response-stratified data exist for the generic population - association strength is the supportable ceiling despite the near-mechanistic biology.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: Clinical NCCL documentation at the hypersensitive teeth with thermal/tactile stimulus testing; exclusion of caries, cracked tooth, pulpitis, and recent whitening/periodontal therapy; habit and dietary history
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Pulpitis and recent restorative or whitening procedures
Gingival recession from periodontal disease (independent pathway)
Anxiety-linked bruxism as a shared driver

evidenceGaps: Clinical NCCL documentation at the hypersensitive teeth with thermal/tactile stimulus testing; exclusion of caries, cracked tooth, pulpitis, and recent whitening/periodontal therapy; habit and dietary history
suggestions.rationale: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY: near-mechanistic biology but epidemiologic support remains cross-sectional co-occurrence with multiple independent DH drivers; no causal claim is forced.

sourceReferences.citation: Zimmer R, Barbosa GF, Portella FF, Soares PV, Reston EG. Association between non-carious cervical lesions, dentin hypersensitivity and anxiety in young adults: A cross-sectional study. J Dent. 2025;153:105563. PMID 39793751.
sourceReferences.note: Cross-sectional cohort (n=157, ages 18-45): DH prevalence 84.7%, NCCL prevalence 49.7%; NCCL was associated with DH at both the one-tooth and more-than-four-teeth thresholds; whitening toothpaste and post-meal brushing also independently associated with DH.
sourceReferences.sourceLocator: PMID 39793751; NCCL-DH co-occurrence and independent habit factors

sourceReferences.citation: Cortellini P, Bissada NF. Mucogingival conditions in the natural dentition: Narrative review, case definitions, and diagnostic considerations. J Periodontol. 2018;89 Suppl 1:S204-S213. PMID 29926948.
sourceReferences.note: Classification review: root-surface exposure from gingival recession is frequently associated with dentinal hypersensitivity and with carious and non-carious cervical lesions; the modern classification records DH presence alongside recession severity and NCCLs.
sourceReferences.sourceLocator: PMID 29926948; recession-NCCL-DH triad in the mucogingival classification

sourceReferences.citation: Sakkaria A, Ramadoss R, Krishnasamy N, Sundar S, Panneerselvam S, Ramani P. Assessment of Nanoscale Configuration of Dentin in Non-carious Cervical Lesions. Cureus. 2023;15(10):e48003. PMID 38034251.
sourceReferences.note: SEM/EDS study: NCCLs are multifactorial (abrasive toothbrushing, occlusal tension, acidic erosion); the authors state NCCLs can be attributed as a predominant factor leading to gingival recession, dentin exposure, and hypersensitivity, while emphasizing the multifactorial etiology.
